540:
An alias is a name that a person goes by that is not their real, official name. It is an alternative name — a second (or third, or fourth) name that someone uses instead of, or alongside, their true identity.

Think of it this way: every person has one real, legal name. An alias is any other name attached to that same person.

Imagine a criminal named Robert King who doesn't want the police to find him. So when he checks into a hotel, he signs in as "Jack Stone." Jack Stone is his alias — a made-up name he uses to hide who he really is.

This is why you'll often hear aliases mentioned in police reports, courtrooms, and crime dramas. The phrase "also known as" — often shortened to a.k.a. — is almost always a sign that an alias is being introduced.

"Robert King, a.k.a. Jack Stone, was arrested on Tuesday."

Here, Jack Stone is the alias.

There are several very different reasons, and the word "alias" is used across all of them:

1. To hide or deceive
This is the most classic use. A person uses a false name to avoid being identified — by the police, a victim, or anyone else looking for them. This is the context where "alias" carries a slightly suspicious or negative tone.

2. For professional or creative purposes
Many writers, musicians, and performers adopt a name that sounds more appealing, memorable, or marketable than their birth name. These are technically aliases too, though in creative fields people often use softer-sounding words like pen name or stage name instead.

  • The author Samuel Clemens wrote under the alias Mark Twain.
  • The musician Stefani Germanotta performs under the alias Lady Gaga.

3. For privacy or personal preference
Some people simply don't want to use their real name in certain situations — online forums, social media, or communities where they prefer anonymity. The username or handle they choose functions as an alias.

4. In computing and technology
In tech, an alias is a shortcut name that points to something else. For example, an email alias is a secondary email address that quietly redirects all incoming messages to a real inbox. The alias address exists and works, but it's just an alternate label for the real one. Similarly, a programmer might create an alias for a long, complex command — a short, easy nickname that triggers the full command when used.
The Key Characteristics of an Alias

No matter the context, an alias always has these features:

  • It is not the original, official name. The alias is always the secondary name, not the primary one.
  • The person behind it remains the same. An alias changes the name, not the individual. Robert King is still Robert King even when he calls himself Jack Stone.
  • It can be self-chosen or given by others. A criminal might choose their own alias, but investigators might also assign a codename or nickname to a suspect — that too counts as an alias.
  • It may or may not be meant to deceive. A stage name is an alias without dishonest intent. A fake name used to evade the law is an alias with clear deceptive intent. The word "alias" covers both.

Because alias is close in meaning to several other words, it helps to know exactly where it sits:

  • Nickname — A casual, affectionate, or descriptive name given to someone (e.g., "Shorty," "Big Red"). A nickname is usually not meant to replace or hide the real name. Aliases can serve this purpose.
  • Pseudonym — A false name adopted specifically for professional or published work (writing, art, performance). A pseudonym is essentially a type of alias, but used in a more specific, creative context. All pseudonyms are aliases, but not all aliases are pseudonyms.
  • Pen name / Stage name — These are even more specific types of pseudonyms (and therefore aliases), used strictly by writers and performers respectively.
  • Codename — A name assigned (usually by an organization) to a person or operation for secrecy. Also a specific type of alias.

So "alias" is the broadest of these terms. It is the umbrella word that can refer to any of the above in the right context.
Whenever you see or hear the word alias, just ask yourself: "Is this the real name, or a stand-in name for the real one?" If it's a stand-in — for any reason, in any field — it's an alias.
541:
An alibi is proof — or a claim — that a person was somewhere else when something bad happened, which means they could not possibly have done it.

The logic is simple: you cannot be in two places at the same time. So if a crime happened in Delhi at 9 PM on Monday, and you were sitting in a restaurant in Mumbai at that exact moment — with witnesses and a receipt to prove it — that is your alibi. It clears you, because it was physically impossible for you to be the one who committed the crime.
Where the Word Belongs: The Legal World

The word "alibi" has its sharpest, most precise meaning in law and criminal investigations.

When the police suspect someone of a crime, one of the first things investigators ask is: "Where were you at the time of the crime?" The answer to that question — if it proves the person was elsewhere — is their alibi.

An alibi does one job in court: it shows that the accused person was not present at the scene of the crime when it happened. And if you weren't there, you couldn't have done it.
What an Alibi Is Made Of

An alibi on its own is just a claim. Saying "I was somewhere else" is not enough. To be believed and accepted — especially in court — an alibi must be backed up by evidence. This evidence is called corroboration (support). Common forms of support include:

  • Witnesses — people who saw you at another location at the relevant time
  • CCTV footage — video that captures you somewhere else
  • Receipts or records — a restaurant bill, hotel check-in, train ticket, or bank transaction that timestamps your location
  • Phone records — calls or data activity from a location far from the crime scene
  • Social media activity — posts or check-ins geotagged at a different place

The stronger and more verifiable the support, the stronger the alibi. An alibi backed by multiple independent witnesses and camera footage is nearly impossible to break down. An alibi that relies only on what a close friend or family member says is considered weak, because people tend to lie for those they love — and investigators know this.

Understanding what makes an alibi strong or weak helps you fully grasp the concept.

A strong alibi is one where:

  • The evidence is hard to fake or dispute
  • The witnesses have no personal reason to lie for the accused
  • Multiple pieces of evidence point to the same conclusion

A weak alibi is one where:

  • Only one person vouches for the accused, especially a friend or family member
  • There is no physical or digital evidence to support the claim
  • The timeline has gaps or inconsistencies

Investigators always probe alibis carefully. They cross-check the claimed location with available records, speak to the witnesses separately to look for contradictions, and examine whether the person could have had enough time to travel from the alibi location to the crime scene and back.
An Important Distinction: Alibi ≠ Just Any Excuse

This is a nuance many learners miss.

An alibi is specifically about location and presence. It answers the question: "Were you there?" — and the answer is no, with proof.

It is not just any explanation or reason for something. For example:

  • "I was sick, so I couldn't submit my homework" — this is an excuse, not an alibi.
  • "I was in the hospital at 3 PM, and here is the admission record to prove it" — when used to show you couldn't have attended something you were blamed for missing, this functions as an alibi.

The core of an alibi is always being elsewhere — a different physical place — at the critical time.

Outside of law, people use the word "alibi" more loosely in everyday conversation to mean any explanation or cover story that gets someone off the hook — even when there is no crime involved.

For example:

  • "My boss asked why I left early, so my colleague gave me an alibi — she told him I had a doctor's appointment."
  • "Do you have an alibi for why you missed the meeting?"

Here, the word is used informally to mean a ready-made explanation or story that protects someone from being blamed or questioned. The idea of being at a different location is less strict in this usage — it can simply mean a convincing reason that explains where you were or what you were doing, so others do not suspect you.

This informal use is very common in conversation, films, and books, so you will encounter it frequently.

The plural of alibi is simply alibis.

"The detective checked all three suspects' alibis."
Quick Examples to Cement Your Understanding

1. Legal context: A woman is accused of robbing a bank at noon on Friday. She produces her office's biometric attendance record, which shows she swiped in at 11:45 AM and swiped out at 1:15 PM that same day. Her office is 40 kilometres from the bank. This is a solid alibi.
  2. Legal context: A man claims he was watching a film at a cinema when a murder occurred. But no one accompanied him, he paid in cash, and there is no camera footage of him there. He has an alibi in name, but it is extremely weak — the kind that investigators will not easily accept.
  3. Informal context: A teenager comes home two hours late. Her parents demand an explanation. She says she was at her friend Priya's house studying, and Priya confirms this by phone. The friend's call is the teenager's "alibi" in this casual, everyday sense.

An alibi is a person's proof — or claim — that they were in a different place at the time something bad happened, making it impossible for them to be responsible for it. In law, it is a formal defence that must be supported by solid evidence. In everyday life, it is used more loosely to mean any explanation or story that keeps someone from being blamed.
542:
To alienate someone means to make them feel like a stranger — disconnected, unwelcome, or pushed away — from a person, a group, a place, or even from themselves.

A useful mental anchor: the word shares its root with "alien," meaning a foreigner or outsider. When you alienate someone, you are, in effect, turning them into an outsider — or making them feel like one.

Meaning 1 — To make someone feel like they don't belong

A person, place, environment, policy, or experience can alienate someone by making them feel isolated, cut off, or disconnected from something they once felt part of.

For example: "The new student felt alienated at school because nobody made an effort to include him." He wasn't physically removed from the school — he was there every day — but emotionally he felt like an outsider, like he didn't belong.

Another example: "Moving abroad can alienate you from your own culture and roots." Over time, you feel a growing distance from the world you came from.

Notice the pattern here — alienate someone from something — you are separated from something you were once connected to.

Meaning 2 — To cause someone to stop liking, supporting, or being loyal to you

This sense is about pushing people away. When your words, actions, or decisions cause others to lose their affection, trust, or goodwill toward you, you have alienated them. They were once on your side; now they are not.

For example: "The politician's dismissive comments alienated many of his supporters." They used to support him — his remarks drove them away.

Another example: "Don't alienate your customers by raising prices without any explanation." Treat them poorly, and they'll walk away.

One important thing to know: you can alienate people intentionally or unintentionally. Most of the time, it happens without the person meaning to — they say the wrong thing, make a thoughtless decision, or behave in a way that quietly drives others away before they even realize it.

These two meanings are two sides of the same coin, and they often happen together.

Meaning 1 is about how the affected person feels — isolated, disconnected, like an outsider.
Meaning 2 is about how a relationship breaks down — loyalty, affection, or support erodes.

In real life, they feed each other: when someone feels like they don't belong (Meaning 1), they naturally withdraw their support or warmth (Meaning 2). And when someone pushes you away (Meaning 2), you begin to feel like you don't belong (Meaning 1). The two collapse into one experience: estrangement.

In formal legal writing, "alienate" can also mean to legally transfer ownership of property or rights to another person — for instance, "He alienated his estate to his heirs before his death." This use is almost never heard in everyday conversation and is confined almost entirely to legal documents. You are unlikely to need to use it yourself, but it's worth knowing so you aren't confused if you encounter it.

These are the most natural ways to use this word:

alienate + someone — "Her aggressive tone alienated everyone in the room."

alienate + someone + from + something/someone — "Years of neglect alienated him from his own family." / "The experience alienated her from the institution she once believed in."

feel/be alienated — "Many young people feel alienated from mainstream politics." / "He felt completely alienated at the party even though he knew everyone there."

The most important of these is the from construction. You are almost always alienated from something — from a community, from a relationship, from a sense of purpose, from society.

"Alienate" sits on the slightly formal side of the vocabulary scale. In casual conversation, people might prefer to say push away, drive away, or cut off. But "alienate" is extremely common in writing, journalism, politics, and professional contexts — you'll regularly see it in sentences like "the policy alienated voters," "the brand is alienating its core audience," or "management practices that alienate employees."

"Alienate" always carries a negative weight. Whether someone is being alienated (made to feel like an outsider) or doing the alienating (pushing others away), the word signals that something has gone wrong — in a relationship, in a community, in a sense of belonging.

Alienated (adjective) — describes how a person feels: disconnected, like an outsider. "She felt profoundly alienated in her own home."

Alienation (noun) — the state or feeling of being cut off and disconnected. "There is a growing sense of alienation among workers who feel the system no longer works for them."

Alienating (adjective) — describes something that causes that feeling of disconnection or pushes people away. "His cold, alienating manner made it hard for anyone to warm to him."
How it differs from similar words

Estrange is the closest synonym. Both words describe emotional distance growing between people. The difference is scope: "estrange" is used almost exclusively for close personal relationships — especially family. You'd say "estranged from his father," but you'd say "alienated voters" or "alienated customers," because "alienate" works on a much wider scale, across large groups and social structures.

Isolate means to cut someone off — to separate them physically or socially until they have no contact. Alienation is subtler and more internal: you can feel deeply alienated while sitting in a crowded room surrounded by people. Isolation is more total and external; alienation is about a feeling.

Distance (as a verb) means to create space — emotional or physical — between people. It's a milder, more neutral word. "Distance yourself from someone" is deliberate and not necessarily harmful. Alienating is heavier: it implies something has been damaged or lost.

To alienate is to create a cold, invisible wall between people — either making someone feel like they don't belong, or causing them to withdraw their warmth and loyalty. It can be done by a single careless remark, by a policy decision, by years of neglect, or by an environment that never made room for someone. The result is always the same: connection breaks down, and someone is left feeling like a stranger.
543:
When someone feels alienated, they feel like they do not belong — like they are an outsider looking in. They feel cut off, separated, or disconnected from something that they are supposed to be a part of.

That "something" can be a person, a group of people, a place, a society, or even their own self.

Think of it this way: imagine you walk into a room full of people who all know each other. They're laughing, sharing jokes, and you understand none of it. You're physically present, but you feel invisible — like you exist in a separate world. That feeling is alienation. You, in that moment, are alienated.

It's not just loneliness. Loneliness is about missing connection. Alienated goes a step further — it's the feeling that you are fundamentally separate from the world around you, that you simply don't fit, or that you've been pushed out.
The Two Directions It Can Go

1. You feel alienated from others.
This means you feel disconnected from the people or society around you. You feel like an outsider, like you don't belong to the group, like the world is moving on without you.

"Growing up in a new country, she felt deeply alienated — she didn't share the culture, the humour, or the references everyone else seemed to live by."

2. You feel alienated from yourself. (Self-alienation)
This is a deeper, more unsettling meaning. Here, a person feels disconnected from their own identity, feelings, or sense of purpose. They feel like a stranger to themselves — like they're going through the motions of life without truly living it, or like the person they've become is not really them.

"After years of doing a job he hated, he felt alienated from himself — he no longer knew what he actually wanted or who he really was."

Both meanings involve the same root feeling: a painful sense of separation.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Alienated" is not a light word. It carries real emotional heaviness. When someone is alienated, they typically feel some combination of:

  • Disconnection — "I am not part of this."
  • Rejection or exclusion — "I have been pushed away, or I was never welcomed."
  • Invisibility — "No one here really sees me or understands me."
  • Estrangement — "Something that was familiar now feels foreign."
  • Powerlessness — "I can't seem to bridge the gap no matter how hard I try."

It's important to understand that alienation isn't always caused by someone actively excluding you. Sometimes, you can feel alienated in a crowd of people who are perfectly kind — simply because you feel that your inner world, your values, or your experiences are too different from everyone else's for any real connection to happen.

In personal/social life:

"He felt alienated at school because his interests were completely different from his classmates'."

Here, it means he felt like he didn't belong socially — like he was on the outside of a group.

In society/politics:

"Many young people feel alienated from mainstream politics — they believe the system doesn't represent them or care about their concerns."

Here, it means they feel cut off from political life — like they have no voice in it, like it doesn't include them.

In the workplace:

"She felt alienated at work after the company changed its culture entirely — the values she had signed up for no longer existed."

Here, she feels estranged from something she once felt connected to. It has drifted away from her, or she from it.

In relationships:

"After the argument, he felt alienated from his closest friend — there was now a strange, cold distance between them."

Here, it describes an emotional gulf that has opened up between two people who were once close.
A Crucial Nuance: Alienated vs. Just "Feeling Left Out"

Feeling left out is temporary and surface-level — you weren't invited to a party, you felt awkward at a dinner. It stings, but it passes.

Alienated is deeper. It suggests a more persistent, more fundamental sense of not belonging — as though the gap between you and the world (or between you and yourself) is structural, not accidental. It's the difference between missing one train and feeling like the trains were never built for you.

The word can describe different intensities:

  • Mildly alienated: "I felt somewhat alienated at the conference — I couldn't connect with anyone."
  • Profoundly alienated: "She felt profoundly alienated from society — like she was living in it but not of it."
  • Completely alienated: "He was completely alienated from his family after decades of unresolved conflict."

The more intense the alienation, the more total the sense of separation.

• "Feel alienated" — the most common usage.
  • "Alienated from society / the world / others / oneself" — notice that "from" almost always follows it when naming what the person is disconnected from.
  • "A sense of alienation" — the noun form used alongside the adjective's context.
  • "Deeply / profoundly alienated" — intensifiers that signal a severe or chronic state.

• It is not the same as being shy or introverted — those are personality traits. A confident extrovert can still feel alienated.
  • It is not the same as being disliked — you can be liked and still feel alienated if the connection feels superficial or false.
  • It is not simply sadness — though sadness can accompany it. Alienation is specifically about the gap between you and something outside (or inside) you.

Alienated describes the painful human experience of disconnection — from others, from society, from meaning, or from oneself. It is the feeling that you are somehow separate from the world you inhabit, and that the distance between you and it is real, persistent, and hard to cross.

It's one of the more emotionally rich words in the English language because it captures something most people have felt at some point in their lives — that quiet, unsettling sense of not quite belonging anywhere.
544:
Think of the word "alien" — something foreign, strange, not belonging. Alienation is the state of feeling like an alien — not literally from outer space, but in an emotional, social, or philosophical sense. It describes the experience of being cut off or separated from something that you would, under normal circumstances, be closely connected to.

What makes alienation a powerful and important word is the implication buried inside it: that this separation is wrong or painful — that a connection should exist, but doesn't. This sense of lost or broken connection is what gives the word its weight.
Meaning 1: Social Alienation — Feeling Like an Outsider

This is the most common everyday meaning. A person who experiences social alienation feels like a stranger — disconnected from the people around them, from their community, or from society at large. They feel they don't belong, aren't understood, or aren't truly seen.

A teenager who moves to a new country and finds nothing familiar — the language, the customs, the jokes — may feel deep alienation. So might someone whose values are completely different from everyone around them, or a person whose personal experiences are so unusual that no one seems to relate.

Here's a crucial distinction: alienation is not the same as loneliness. Loneliness is the pain of being alone. Alienation is the feeling of being a stranger — even when you are surrounded by people. You can sit in a crowded room, at a party full of people, and feel utterly alienated — invisible, disconnected, out of place. The crowd makes no difference to alienation.
Meaning 2: Self-Alienation — Feeling Like a Stranger to Yourself

Alienation can also turn inward. Self-alienation is the experience of being cut off not from others, but from yourself — from your own identity, your values, your desires, or your emotions.

A person experiencing this feels like their life doesn't truly belong to them. They go through the motions — working, socializing, performing roles — but none of it feels genuinely theirs. There's a glass wall between them and their own experience. They might feel that their real self has been buried under pressure from society, family expectations, or circumstance.

This kind of alienation is a major theme in existentialist philosophy and psychology. It is closely related to the psychological concept of depersonalization — where a person feels detached from their own mind or body, like watching themselves from the outside. Writers like Franz Kafka, whose characters often find themselves trapped in systems and identities they didn't choose, are famous for portraying this kind of alienation in fiction.
Meaning 3: Alienation from Work — The Sociological/Marxist Sense

The philosopher and economist Karl Marx gave alienation one of its most influential specific meanings. He argued that workers in a capitalist economic system experience alienation because they are completely disconnected from the products they create and the work they do.

Imagine a factory worker who spends twelve hours a day tightening a single bolt on a machine, over and over. He doesn't design the machine, doesn't understand the bigger picture, doesn't own the machine, and has no say in what happens to it. The final product — the machine — is taken away and sold by someone else for profit. The worker himself is treated less like a human being and more like a tool.

Marx described this alienation as happening on four levels. The worker becomes alienated from the product of their labor (it doesn't belong to them), from the act of working (it feels mechanical and meaningless, not fulfilling or creative), from other people (competition and hierarchy break down genuine human connection), and from their own human potential (work under such conditions prevents them from expressing their intelligence, creativity, and full humanity).

You don't need to agree with Marx's broader political views to find this idea useful. The core insight — that people can feel deeply disconnected from their own work, that their labor can feel like something that has nothing to do with who they truly are — is widely recognized across sociology, psychology, and organizational studies. When someone says "I'm just a number here" or "I feel like a machine at this job," they are describing exactly this kind of alienation.
Meaning 4: Legal Alienation — The Transfer of Property

In law, "alienation" has a completely different meaning that has nothing to do with feelings or philosophy. Here, it simply means the legal transfer of ownership — of property, land, or rights — from one person to another.

If a contract says "there shall be no alienation of this property without written consent," it means the property cannot be sold, given away, or transferred to someone else without permission. This is a formal, technical legal term. You are most likely to encounter it in property law, contracts, and older legal documents.

Alienation vs. isolation. Isolation is a situation — you are physically or socially separated from others. Alienation is an inner experience — the feeling of not belonging. A hermit who loves solitude is isolated but not alienated. A person surrounded by busy colleagues they feel no connection with is alienated but not isolated.

Alienation vs. estrangement. Estrangement usually refers to a specific relationship that has broken down — "she is estranged from her father." It's personal and particular. Alienation tends to be broader — a more general condition of disconnection from the world, from society, or from oneself. The two words overlap, but estrangement is more specific while alienation is more all-encompassing.

Alienation implies a breach of something expected. This is the key nuance that ties all the non-legal meanings together. If you feel alienated from your workplace, it's not just that you dislike it — there's an implied sense that human beings should find meaning and connection in their work, and yours has been stripped of that. If you feel alienated from society, there's an underlying sense that belonging and community are natural human needs, and yours are going unmet. Alienation always implies a gap between how things are and how they ought to be.

Understanding the family of the word rounds out your knowledge. Alienated is the adjective ("she felt deeply alienated"). To alienate is the verb — it means either to cause someone to feel alienated ("his cold behavior alienated his friends") or, in law, to transfer property. Alienating describes something that causes the feeling ("an alienating work environment").

Alienation, in its non-legal sense, is the state of being cut off or separated from something you are naturally meant to be connected to — whether that's other people, society, your work, or your own self. It carries a sense of loss, wrongness, and distance. The deeper the expected connection, the more painful the alienation. In law, by contrast, it simply means the transfer of ownership from one party to another — a technical term with no emotional meaning at all.
545: "Alight" as an adjective means on fire or glowing with light. It describes something that is actively lit up — whether by real flames, by bright light, or even by a strong emotion radiating from within a person.

When something is "alight," it is burning — it has caught fire and is in an active state of burning.

  • The dry leaves were alight within seconds.
  • By the time help arrived, the entire roof was alight.

This is slightly different from simply saying something "caught fire." "Alight" describes the ongoing state of burning — the thing is currently burning, right now. A lit candle is alight. A burning haystack is alight.
Meaning 2: Glowing with light / Radiant with brightness

"Alight" can describe something that is brilliantly lit up and radiating light, even without actual fire. It suggests a vivid, active glow — not dim or ordinary light, but something that seems alive and shining.

  • The night sky was alight with a thousand stars.
  • The city was alight with fireworks on New Year's Eve.
  • The whole street was alight with lanterns during the festival.

Notice the key idea: this is not just "lit" or "bright" — "alight" carries a sense of something radiating light energetically, as if the light has a life of its own.

This is the most beautiful and expressive use of the word. When a person's face, eyes, or expression is described as "alight," it means they are so full of a strong positive emotion that it visibly shines through them — as if they are lit from within.

  • Her eyes were alight with excitement as she unwrapped the gift.
  • His face was alight with pride when his daughter walked across the stage.
  • The children's faces were alight with wonder at the fireworks.

Two things to notice here:

First, "alight" in this sense is almost always used for positive, energising emotions — joy, excitement, wonder, passion, love. You would not say someone's face was "alight with sadness" or "alight with boredom." The word carries warmth and energy.

Second, the emotion must be visibly radiating outward. You can't feel "alight" privately inside your chest. "Alight" describes what other people can see on your face or in your eyes — the way strong emotion shows itself outwardly, like a glow you cannot hide.
A critical grammar rule: "alight" never goes before a noun

This is one of the most important things to know about this word. "Alight" is what linguists call a predicative adjective — it must always appear after a linking verb (like is, was, looked, seemed, became), never directly before the noun it describes.

✅ Correct: The building was alight.
✅ Correct: Her face looked alight with joy.
✅ Correct: The sky seemed alight.

❌ Incorrect: the alight building
❌ Incorrect: her alight face

This pattern is shared by several English adjectives that begin with "a-" — words like asleep, alive, awake, afraid, ashamed, alone, afoot. You say "she was asleep" but never "the asleep woman." "Alight" follows the exact same rule.

You will very frequently see "alight" in the phrase "set (something) alight", which means to cause something to start burning — to put fire to it.

  • The arsonist set the warehouse alight.
  • A single spark can set dry timber alight.

This phrase works exactly like "set on fire" — they are interchangeable in meaning. "Set alight" is particularly common in British English.
The overall feel and tone of the word

"Alight" is not a neutral or flat word. It carries a sense of energy, vividness, and life. Whatever is described as "alight" is never dull or still — it is actively radiating something outward. Fire, light, or emotion — "alight" always suggests something that is alive and expressive.

This is why the word works so naturally for emotions. When you say someone's eyes are "alight with excitement," you are painting a picture of someone so full of feeling that it practically glows off of them. The word does something that a phrase like "she was very excited" cannot — it makes you see the emotion rather than just understand it intellectually.

The word also tends to carry a slightly elevated, literary quality. "The building was alight" sounds a little more vivid and dramatic than the plain "the building was on fire." Writers and journalists often choose "alight" precisely for this reason — it adds intensity without adding extra words.

• Ablaze — also means on fire or lit up, but usually suggests a larger, more intense fire or light than "alight." A city after bombing might be "ablaze"; a single candle is "alight," not "ablaze."
  • Aglow — very similar to "alight" in the light and emotion senses, but softer and gentler. "Aglow" feels warm and quiet; "alight" feels more vivid and active.
  • Illuminated — simply means lit up by a light source. It is neutral and descriptive, with no emotional energy. "Alight" always carries more intensity.
  • Radiant — when describing a person glowing with emotion, "radiant" is close in meaning, but it focuses on the beauty of the glow. "Alight" focuses on the energy and intensity of the emotion showing through.

"Alight" (adjective) means one of three things, all connected by the same core idea of something actively radiating outward:

  1. On fire — actually burning with flames (the cabin was alight)
  2. Glowing with light — brilliantly and actively lit up (the sky was alight with stars)
  3. Glowing with emotion — visibly radiating a strong positive feeling (her face was alight with joy)

Always used after a linking verb, never before the noun. Very commonly seen in the phrase "set alight." Carries a tone of vividness, energy, and active radiance in all its uses.
546: Both meanings of "alight" share one beautiful underlying idea: something in motion comes gently to rest in a specific place. Keep that image in your mind — it ties everything together.
Meaning 1 — To land and settle on a surface

This is the most physical meaning. It describes the moment when something — most commonly a bird or insect — comes down through the air and settles on a spot.

  • A sparrow alighted on the fence post.
  • The butterfly alighted on the rose.
  • Snowflakes alighted on her coat.

It is also used for a person stepping off a vehicle — a bus, train, or carriage. This use is formal and common in British English, especially in transport announcements.

  • Passengers should alight at the next stop.
  • She alighted from the train and looked around the unfamiliar station.

In both cases — bird landing, person stepping off — the action is the same in spirit: movement ends, and something comes to rest somewhere.
Meaning 2 — To come across something, often by chance

This meaning is mental rather than physical. When your eyes or mind "alight on" something, you suddenly notice it or discover it — often unexpectedly, as if you stumbled upon it without planning to.

Think of your attention as a bird flying around a room — and then suddenly landing on one particular thing. That landing is what "alight on" means here.

  • Her eyes alighted on a dusty envelope at the back of the drawer.
  • While flipping through the book, he alighted on a passage that changed his thinking.
  • After hours of searching, she finally alighted on the perfect solution.

Notice that this meaning almost always uses the preposition "on" or "upon" — you alight on something, or alight upon something.

• Alight on / alight upon → used for both meanings (landing on a surface, or noticing something)
  • Alight from → used specifically for stepping off a vehicle
Register — when is this word used?

"Alight" as a verb is literary and formal. You will rarely hear it in everyday conversation. It lives mostly in literature, formal writing, and official announcements. In casual speech, people simply say:

  • landed on — instead of alighted on (for birds/insects)
  • got off — instead of alighted from (for vehicles)
  • noticed or came across — instead of alighted on (for discovering something)

So when you encounter "alight" as a verb, it is almost always a deliberate, stylish word choice — the writer wants a sense of gentleness, precision, or elegance.
Do not confuse it with the adjective "alight"

The word "alight" is also commonly used as an adjective, and it means something completely different — on fire, or glowing with light. This can trip up learners.

  • The building was alight. (= on fire)
  • Her face was alight with happiness. (= glowing, radiant)

The context will always make it clear. If something or someone is doing the action, it is the verb. If the word is describing a state, it is the adjective. You will never genuinely confuse the two once you understand both.
A note on the past tense

The standard past tense is alighted.

  • The bird alighted on the branch. ✓

In older or very literary texts, you may occasionally see alit used as an irregular past tense form. It is rare and old-fashioned, but worth knowing so it does not surprise you.

  • The bird alit on the branch. (old-fashioned)

Physical meaningTo come down and land/settle on something; or to step off a vehicle
Mental meaningTo notice or discover something, often by chance (alight on/upon)
ToneFormal and literary
Key prepositionson, upon (for both meanings) · from (for vehicles)
Don't confuse withThe adjective "alight" = on fire / glowing

The word carries a quiet elegance — the image of something landing softly and precisely, whether a bird on a branch, a traveller stepping off a train, or a curious mind landing on an idea.
547:
Aligned means "properly arranged so that things match up, point in the same direction, or agree with each other."

Whether you're talking about physical objects or abstract ideas like goals and values, the word always carries the same underlying image: things that are in line with each other — not crooked, not out of place, not working against each other.

1. Physical Alignment — things positioned correctly in a line or in proper relation to each other

This is the most literal meaning. When something is aligned, it sits in exactly the right position relative to something else — straight, even, and correct.

Examples:

  • "The wheels of the car are aligned." → The wheels point perfectly straight, not angled to the left or right. If they weren't aligned, the car would pull to one side.
  • "The text on this page is aligned to the left." → Every line of text starts at the same left edge, forming a neat vertical line.
  • "The holes in the two pieces of metal are aligned." → The holes line up perfectly so a bolt can pass through both.
  • "The planets are aligned." → Several planets happen to form a straight line when viewed from a certain point.

In all these cases, the opposite — misaligned — means things are off, crooked, or out of proper position.

2. Abstract Alignment — things that are in agreement, harmony, or working toward the same purpose

This is the more commonly used sense in everyday modern life. Here, "aligned" doesn't describe physical position but rather the relationship between ideas, goals, values, interests, or people. When two things are aligned, they are pointing in the same direction — not in conflict, not pulling apart.

Examples:

  • "Our goals are aligned." → You and I want the same things; we're working toward the same outcome.
  • "The team is aligned on the new strategy." → Everyone on the team understands and agrees with the plan; there's no internal disagreement.
  • "Her personal values and her company's values are aligned." → What she believes in matches what the company stands for. There's no friction or contradiction between the two.
  • "The incentives are aligned." → The rewards or motivations are set up in a way that naturally encourages everyone to work together toward the same result.
  • "My expectations were not aligned with reality." → What I expected didn't match what actually happened.

The opposite — not aligned or misaligned — means a mismatch, a conflict, or a disconnect. For example, "misaligned incentives" means people are being rewarded for doing things that don't actually benefit the overall goal.

3. Political or Ideological Alignment — associated with or on the side of a particular group or cause

"Aligned" is also used to describe which side a person, country, or organization supports or is associated with. In this sense, "aligned with X" means "on X's side" or "sharing X's position or interests."

Examples:

  • "During the Cold War, many countries were aligned with either the United States or the Soviet Union." → Those countries had chosen a side; they shared interests, received support from, and cooperated with one of the two powers.
  • "Non-aligned nations" → Countries that deliberately chose not to take sides with either major power. (This is also where the famous "Non-Aligned Movement" gets its name.)
  • "He is aligned with the progressive wing of the party." → He shares that group's views and is politically associated with them.
  • "The newspaper is aligned with conservative values." → It consistently supports and reflects conservative positions.

Across all three uses, notice the same idea running through them:

Things that are aligned are not in conflict, not crooked, not pulling in different directions — they are in agreement, in order, and pointing the same way.

Whether it's car wheels, personal values, or nations in a war — alignment always means a kind of harmony of direction.

"Aligned" isn't all-or-nothing. You'll often see it modified:

  • Fully / completely aligned → perfect agreement or positioning, no gaps at all
  • Closely / well aligned → in strong agreement, even if not perfect
  • Broadly aligned → mostly in agreement on the big things, perhaps with some minor differences
  • Partially aligned → some overlap in direction, but also some differences
  • Poorly aligned / misaligned → significant mismatch or conflict

Example:

"The two departments are broadly aligned on the budget, but they have some disagreements on the timeline."

• "aligned with" → in agreement or association with something specific (aligned with our mission, aligned with their interests)
  • "aligned on" → in agreement about a specific topic (aligned on the next steps, aligned on priorities)
  • "stay aligned" → continue to remain in agreement as things evolve (We need to stay aligned as the project changes.)
  • "get aligned" → reach a state of agreement (Let's get aligned before the meeting.)
  • "alignment" (the noun) → the state or condition of being aligned (We need to achieve alignment across all teams.)

SenseWhat it meansExample
PhysicalCorrectly positioned in a straight line or proper relationaligned wheels, aligned text
AbstractIn agreement, harmony, or working toward the same goalaligned values, aligned teams
Political/IdeologicalOn the same side as, associated withaligned with the West

The word "aligned" is powerful precisely because it works both for the world you can see — objects in a line — and the world of ideas — people in agreement. Once you hear it, ask yourself: aligned in position, or aligned in purpose? That question will unlock the meaning every time.
548:
Alignment means the condition of things being correctly lined up, positioned, or arranged in relation to each other. Think of it as things pointing in the same direction, fitting together properly, or being in the right relationship with one another — whether physically or in terms of ideas, goals, and values.

The word carries two broad types of meaning: a literal, physical sense and a figurative, abstract sense. Both are used constantly in everyday life.

When used in a physical or spatial sense, alignment refers to things being arranged in a straight line or in the correct relative position so that they work properly together.

Examples:

  • The wheels of a car are said to be in alignment when they are all pointing perfectly straight and at the correct angles. When they drift out of alignment, the car pulls to one side and the tires wear unevenly.
  • A dentist might talk about the alignment of your teeth — whether they line up correctly when you bite down.
  • A printer produces crisp, clean text when the ink heads are in alignment. If they're off, the letters look blurry or doubled.
  • In construction, bricklayers check the alignment of each row of bricks to make sure they form a perfectly straight wall.
  • In astronomy, an alignment occurs when celestial bodies like the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up — which is what causes a solar eclipse.

The key idea in all these cases: things have a "correct" or "intended" position relative to each other, and alignment is the state of being in that correct position.

This is where the word really opens up. In its abstract sense, alignment means agreement, harmony, or coordination between people, ideas, goals, values, or organizations. Instead of objects lining up in space, it's about things pointing in the same direction conceptually.

Think of it this way: just like car wheels need to point in the same direction for the car to drive smoothly, people or groups need to "point in the same direction" — share the same goals or values — to work well together. That's alignment.

Examples:

  • If a company's strategy and its employees' daily actions are in alignment, everyone is working toward the same goals, and nothing is wasted.
  • If your personal values and your job are in alignment, you find your work meaningful and fulfilling.
  • Two friends are in alignment when they agree on the plan: what to do, where to go, and what they each expect.
  • Politicians who share similar beliefs are said to have the same political alignment.

The key idea in all these cases: there is agreement, consistency, or coordination — no contradiction, no conflict, no pulling in opposite directions.

Alignment is not just about agreeing. It also implies a kind of purposeful correctness — not just that things happen to match, but that they are arranged or coordinated in the way they should be for the best outcome. This is why "alignment" feels stronger and more meaningful than just "agreement."

Also important: alignment is a condition, not an action. The action is "to align." The condition (the state of having been aligned, or being aligned) is "alignment." So when someone says "we achieved alignment," they mean they reached a state where things were properly coordinated.

Alignment is not always all-or-nothing. Things can be:

  • In full alignment — perfectly matched, coordinated, or lined up.
  • In partial alignment — mostly matching, but with some gaps or differences.
  • Out of alignment (or in misalignment) — noticeably off, conflicting, or contradicting each other.

For example, two business partners might be in partial alignment — they agree on the goal but disagree on the method. A car's wheels might be slightly out of alignment — not dangerously off, but enough to cause long-term problems.
Where You Will Commonly Encounter This Word

In mechanics and engineering: wheel alignment, spinal alignment, gear alignment — always about physical positioning.

In business and organizations: "strategic alignment" means all departments are working toward the same strategy. "Alignment between teams" means they are coordinating properly and not working at cross-purposes.

In personal life: "alignment with your values" means your actions and beliefs are consistent with each other. If you value honesty but tell lies regularly, you are out of alignment with your own values.

In politics: "political alignment" refers to where a person or group stands ideologically — which side, party, or set of beliefs they are associated with.

In technology and AI: "alignment" (especially "AI alignment") refers to the challenge of making AI systems act in accordance with human values and intentions — making sure AI's behavior "lines up" with what humans actually want and consider good.

In design and typography: text or images can be left-aligned, right-aligned, or center-aligned — meaning they line up along the left edge, right edge, or center of a page.

The opposite of alignment is misalignment — the condition of things being out of correct position, out of agreement, or not coordinated. Misalignment always implies something is off, and usually implies that this mismatch is causing a problem.
One Unifying Way to Think About It

No matter the context — physical or abstract — alignment always answers the same question: "Are these things in the right relationship with each other?" When the answer is yes, you have alignment. When the answer is no, you have misalignment. The word is always about the relationship between two or more things, and whether that relationship is correct, coordinated, and pointing in the same direction.
549: "Alike" means similar — two or more things or people share the same, or nearly the same, qualities, features, or characteristics. When you say two things are "alike," you are saying they noticeably resemble each other in some meaningful way.
The Single Most Important Grammar Rule

This is what makes "alike" unique among adjectives, and getting this right will set you apart from many learners.

"Alike" is a predicative adjective. This means it can only appear after a linking verb (like is, are, look, seem, appear, feel). It can never appear directly before a noun to describe it.

✅ "The two sisters are alike."
✅ "These problems look alike to me."

❌ "They are alike sisters."
❌ "It was an alike situation."

Think of it this way: "alike" is a conclusion you arrive at after observing the subjects — not a label you stick in front of a noun.

"Alike" almost always involves at least two things being compared. You are not describing one thing in isolation — you are saying that two or more things resemble each other. This is a relational word. It describes the relationship between subjects, not any single subject alone.

This is why "alike" most naturally pairs with a plural subject:

"The twins are alike." (two people)
"All three paintings are alike in style." (three things)

It can work with a singular subject too, but then you must state what the second thing is:

"She is alike in temperament to her mother."

"Alike" does not mean exactly the same in every way. It means similar in notable ways. Two things that are alike share important features — but they may still differ in other respects.

For example: "The two brothers are alike — both are quiet, hardworking, and passionate about music." They are alike in those key traits, but they might still look different, have different hobbies, or disagree on other things.

If you want to say two things are exactly the same in every possible way, "identical" is the right word, not "alike."

"Same" means two things are one and the same — as if they are not truly separate ("We read the same book" — the exact same book). "Alike" only says they are similar, not that they are the exact same object or entity.

These two words are close in meaning and often interchangeable. The key practical difference is grammatical: "similar" can appear before a noun ("a similar problem"), but "alike" cannot ("an alike problem" is wrong). "Alike" also tends to sound slightly more emphatic — as if the similarity is particularly striking or worth remarking on.

On its own, "alike" implies a clear, noticeable similarity — not a trivial or barely-there one. You typically use it when the resemblance is meaningful enough to be worth pointing out.

You can adjust the degree with intensifiers:

  • "very alike" — strongly similar
  • "strikingly alike" — the similarity is surprising or remarkable
  • "remarkably alike" — impressively similar
  • "somewhat alike" / "a little alike" — only partially similar

Pattern 1: [Plural subject] + [linking verb] + alike
"The two designs are alike."
"These methods look alike on the surface."

Pattern 2: [Subject] + [linking verb] + alike + in + [specific aspect]
"The two cousins are alike in their sense of humor."
"These two languages are alike in structure."

This "in" pattern is very useful when you want to be precise about which aspect the things are alike in.

Anything that can be compared — people, animals, objects, ideas, situations, methods, styles, personalities, opinions, and so on.

"The two dogs are alike — both are gentle and playful."
"Your situation and mine are alike."
"Their political views are alike."

"Alike" = similar in a meaningful way, always used after a linking verb, always involving a comparison between two or more things, and never placed directly before a noun. It does not mean identical, and it does not mean exactly the same. It points to resemblance — significant enough to notice and worth saying out loud.
